1.1 Survival Function


  • The survival function of T is s(t) = P(T > t), t ≥ 0


    • s(0) = 1, s(∞) = 0


    • Decreasing-Function


  • Treatment(1) & Placebo(0):


    • s(t) = P(T > t | X)

      • s₁(t) = P(T > t | X = 1)

      • s₀(t) = P(T > t | X = 0)


  • Comparison of Survival Curves


    • Dominated Survival Curves


    • Crossed Survival Curves


    • Overlapped survival curves


  • Dominated Curve

1.2 Hazard Function


  • h(t) ≈ P(T = t | T ≥ t)


  • h(t) ≥ 0


  • h(t) ~ s(t)


  • s(t) = exp( - H(t)), H(t): Cumulative hazard function.


    • \(H(t) = \int_0^t h(u) du\)


  • h(t) is more interpretable than s(t)


1.3 Survival Curve


  • Observed Time(Z)


    • Z = Event Time, Censoring Status = 1


    • Z = Censoring Time, Censoring Status = 0


    • Z = Min(Event Time, Censoring Time)


  • Censored Data


    • Censored Data: \(\big( Z_{i}, \delta_{i}, X_{i} \big) , i = 1, ..., n\)


    • \(\delta\): Censoring Status


  • To plot s(t) based on censored data


1.4 Kaplan-Meier(KM) Estimator


  • KM Estimator for \(\ \hat{ s_{(t)} }\)


  • Plot \(\ \hat{ s_{(t)} }\ \) based on censored data


    • KM has jumps at Event-Time only


    • \(h( z_{j}) = \frac{no.\ Event \ at \ z_{j}}{no. \ at \ risk \ at \ z_{j}}\)


      • \(no. \ : \ number \ of \ ...\)


      • \(no. \ at \ risk \ at \ z_{j} \ : \ RiskSet \ at \ z_{j}\)


      • “The size of the risk set directly reflects the number of individuals still under observation at a given time point. As time progresses, the risk set gradually diminishes due to events or censoring. This implies that estimates at later time points (such as survival rates or cumulative hazard) may be based on a smaller sample, leading to a decrease in the stability of these estimates.”


      • “If the number of individuals at risk at a certain time point falls below 10, the survival curve beyond that point may become unstable and subject to greater fluctuation.” —— one-in-ten rule (or the 10 EPV rule)


    • \(\ \hat{ s_{(t)} }\ \) goes to 0 if the maximum of Z is an Event


  • Plot \(\ \hat{ s_{(t)} }\ \) based on censored data With RiskSet

1.5 Log-Rank Test


  • Null Hypothesis: s₀(t) = s₁(t)


    • Estimated Hazard of h₀ ≈ Estimated Hazard of h₁ ≈ Estimated Hazard of (h₀ .and. h₁)


    • \(LR\ \sim \ \chi _{df} ( \alpha )\)


      • LR = Sum( difference of h )


    • Reject H₀ while \(LR\ < \ \chi _{df} ( \alpha )\)


  • Effect Size


    • ∆RMST(Restricted Mean Survival Time Difference)


    • Hazard Ratio(HR)


    • Log-Rank(LR) Test Effect-Size


  • Weighted LR Test


    • Weighted Log-Rank Test


1.6 Cox Proportional Hazard(PH) Model


  • Cox PH Model for h(t | X)


  • HR = exp(coef.)


  • Application of the Cox PH Model

  • (The study hypothesizes that the independent variable is associated with the risk of the event and remains an independent predictor after controlling for potential confounders.)


  • Univariate Cox PH Model


    • The univariate Cox proportional hazards model was used to explore the association between each variable and the time-to-event outcome.


    • This step focuses on the direction and magnitude of the association between individual variables and the event risk.


  • Multivariable Cox PH Model

  • The multivariable Cox proportional hazards model was applied to evaluate whether the main independent variable is an independent predictor of the outcome.


    • Model 1 (Unadjusted model):Time ~ Independent


    • Model 2 (Partially adjusted model):Time ~ Independent + demographic variables


    • Model 3 (Fully adjusted model):Time ~ Independent + demographic variables + potential confounders


    • Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported for all models.


  • Interpretation:


    • By comparing the results across models, the stability of the association was assessed.


    • If the independent variable remained statistically significant in the fully adjusted model, it was considered an independent predictor of the outcome.


  • All Cox models were fitted under the proportional hazards assumption.


  • Interpretion of Hazard Ratio(HR)
